claim: SARS-CoV-2 has been spreading around the world for the past year.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has been spreading around the world for the past year.
evidence: This is a temporal statement about the pandemic that is stated in the abstract without specific data or citation.

claim: B.1.1.7 (alpha), B.1.351 (beta), and P.1 (gamma) variants share a key mutation N501Y on the receptor-binding domain (RBD).
source: Recently, several variants such as B.1.1.7 (alpha), B.1.351 (beta), and P.1 (gamma), which share a key mutation N501Y on the receptor-binding domain (RBD), appear to be more infectious to humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 variants and their genetic characteristics.

claim: B.1.1.7 (alpha), B.1.351 (beta), and P.1 (gamma) variants appear to be more infectious to humans.
source: Recently, several variants such as B.1.1.7 (alpha), B.1.351 (beta), and P.1 (gamma), which share a key mutation N501Y on the receptor-binding domain (RBD), appear to be more infectious to humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by epidemiological knowledge about these variants.

claim: RBD with the N501Y mutation exhibited a considerably stronger interaction with ACE2, with a faster association rate and a slower dissociation rate.
source: Remarkably, RBD with the N501Y mutation exhibited a considerably stronger interaction, with a faster association rate and a slower dissociation rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell surface-binding assays and kinetics studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: AFM-based single-molecule force microscopy quantified the interaction strength of RBD with the N501Y mutation as having increased binding probability and requiring increased unbinding force.
source: Atomic force microscopy (AFM)-based single-molecule force microscopy (SMFS) consistently quantified the interaction strength of RBD with the mutation as having increased binding probability and requiring increased unbinding force.
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N501Y mutation introduced additional π-π and π-cation interactions that could explain the changes observed by force microscopy.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of RBD–ACE2 complexes indicated that the N501Y mutation introduced additional π-π and π-cation interactions that could explain the changes observed by force microscopy.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reinforced RBD–ACE2 interaction resulting from the N501Y mutation should play an essential role in the higher rate of transmission of SARS-CoV-2 variants.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the reinforced RBD–ACE2 interaction that results from the N501Y mutation in the RBD should play an essential role in the higher rate of transmission of SARS-CoV-2 variants, and that future mutations in the RBD of the virus should be under surveillance.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing stronger RBD-ACE2 binding.

claim: Future mutations in the RBD of the virus should be under surveillance.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the reinforced RBD–ACE2 interaction that results from the N501Y mutation in the RBD should play an essential role in the higher rate of transmission of SARS-CoV-2 variants, and that future mutations in the RBD of the virus should be under surveillance.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings about the N501Y mutation's impact.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 emerged in humans in 2003 after being transferred from an animal reservoir.
source: In 2003, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1) emerged in humans after being transferred from an animal reservoir and infected over 8000 people with a fatality rate of ~10% fatality rate (Ksiazek et al., 2003; Florindo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 infected over 8000 people with a fatality rate of ~10%.
source: In 2003, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1) emerged in humans after being transferred from an animal reservoir and infected over 8000 people with a fatality rate of ~10% fatality rate (Ksiazek et al., 2003; Florindo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MERS-CoV has infected over 1700 people with a fatality rate of ~36% since 2012.
source: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) has infected over 1700 people with a fatality rate of ~36% since 2012 (Zaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 was identified as the cause of an outbreak of a new respiratory illness named COVID-19 in late December 2019.
source: In late December 2019, a novel coronavirus, called severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), was identified as the cause of an outbreak of a new respiratory illness named COVID-19.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has caused more than 4 million deaths to date.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has caused more than 4 million deaths to date.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the pandemic death toll at the time of writing.

claim: Coronaviruses are large, enveloped, positive-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the coronaviridae family.
source: Coronaviruses are large, enveloped, positive-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the coronaviridae family, which comprises four genera: alpha-coronaviruses, beta-coronaviruses, gamma-coronaviruses, and delta-coronaviruses (Zumla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The coronaviridae family comprises four genera: alpha-coronaviruses, beta-coronaviruses, gamma-coronaviruses, and delta-coronaviruses.
source: Coronaviruses are large, enveloped, positive-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the coronaviridae family, which comprises four genera: alpha-coronaviruses, beta-coronaviruses, gamma-coronaviruses, and delta-coronaviruses (Zumla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1, and MERS-CoV are beta-coronaviruses that infect mammalians.
source: SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1, and MERS-CoV, which infect mammalians (Wu et al., 2020), are beta-coronaviruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Envelope-anchored spike proteins mediate coronavirus entry into host cells by first binding to a specific host receptor and then fusing the viral and host membranes.
source: Envelope-anchored spike proteins are capable of mediating coronavirus entry into host cells by first binding to a specific host receptor and then fusing the viral and host membranes (Wu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The coronavirus spike protein is a class I fusion protein.
source: The coronavirus spike protein, a class I fusion protein, is synthesized as a precursor single polypeptide chain consisting of three segments: a large ectodomain, a single-pass transmembrane anchor, and a short intracellular tail (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronavirus spike protein structure.

claim: The coronavirus spike protein is synthesized as a precursor single polypeptide chain consisting of three segments: a large ectodomain, a single-pass transmembrane anchor, and a short intracellular tail.
source: The coronavirus spike protein, a class I fusion protein, is synthesized as a precursor single polypeptide chain consisting of three segments: a large ectodomain, a single-pass transmembrane anchor, and a short intracellular tail (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The spike protein is cleaved into an amino-terminal subunit (S1) and a carboxyl-terminal subunit (S2) by host furin-like proteases after interacting with the host receptor.
source: After interacting with the host receptor, the spike protein is cleaved into an amino-terminal subunit (S1) and a carboxyl-terminal subunit (S2) by host furin-like proteases (Yuan et al., 2017; Li, 2016; Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) located in the C-terminal region of the S1 subunit is responsible for recognizing and binding the host receptor.
source: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) located in the C-terminal region of the S1 subunit (S1 CTD) is responsible for recognizing and binding the host receptor and is critical in determining the cell tropism, host range, and zoonotic transmission of coronaviruses (Wu et al., 2020; Li, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The RBD is critical in determining the cell tropism, host range, and zoonotic transmission of coronaviruses.
source: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) located in the C-terminal region of the S1 subunit (S1 CTD) is responsible for recognizing and binding the host receptor and is critical in determining the cell tropism, host range, and zoonotic transmission of coronaviruses (Wu et al., 2020; Li, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The S2 subunit contains a hydrophobic fusion loop for membrane fusion.
source: The S2 subunit contains a hydrophobic fusion loop for membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronavirus spike protein structure.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have illuminated the prefusion and postfusion structures of the SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins.
source: Cryo-EM studies have illuminated the prefusion and postfusion structures of the SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins, implying that coronaviruses undergo conformational changes during infection.
evidence: This claim refers to established structural biology studies.

claim: Coronaviruses undergo conformational changes during infection.
source: Cryo-EM studies have illuminated the prefusion and postfusion structures of the SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins, implying that coronaviruses undergo conformational changes during infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural studies showing different conformational states.

claim: The spike protein forms a clove-shaped homotrimer with three S1 heads and a trimeric S2 stalk.
source: The spike protein forms a clove-shaped homotrimer with three S1 heads and a trimeric S2 stalk.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spike protein structure.

claim: Spike protein utilizes the CTD1 as the RBD, which changes from the 'down' conformation to the 'up' conformation to allow for receptor binding.
source: Structural comparisons indicated that spike protein utilizes the CTD1 (N-terminal domain in CTD) as the RBD, which changes from the 'down' conformation to the 'up' conformation and then converts from the inactivated state to the activated state to allow for receptor binding, and possibly also to initiate subsequent conformational changes of the S2 subunits to mediate membrane fusion (Yuan et al., 2017; Li, 2016; Lan et al., 2020; Kirchdoerfer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: The binding of spike RBD to SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2 is the first step in viral entry into the host cell.
source: The binding of spike RBD to SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2 is the first step in viral entry into the host cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the viral entry mechanism.

claim: The majority of vaccines and neutralizing antibodies under development target the RBD region.
source: Thus, the majority of vaccines and neutralizing antibodies that are under development target this region.
evidence: This is knowledge about vaccine and therapeutic development strategies.

claim: The B.1.1.7 variant was first detected in the United Kingdom in September 2020.
source: The alpha variant (B.1.1.7 lineage) was first detected in the United Kingdom in September 2020, and another variant (B.1.351 lineage, beta) was first detected in October 2020 in the Republic of South Africa (Rahimi and Talebi Bezmin Abadi, 2021; Greaney et al., 2021; CNBC, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published sources.

claim: The B.1.351 variant was first detected in October 2020 in the Republic of South Africa.
source: The alpha variant (B.1.1.7 lineage) was first detected in the United Kingdom in September 2020, and another variant (B.1.351 lineage, beta) was first detected in October 2020 in the Republic of South Africa (Rahimi and Talebi Bezmin Abadi, 2021; Greaney et al., 2021; CNBC, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published sources.

claim: Both B.1.1.7 and B.1.351 variants carry an N501Y mutation.
source: Both of these mutants carry an N501Y mutation, and the B.1.351 lineage has two additional mutations (K417N and E484K) within the RBD region (Figure 1B,C; Leung et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The B.1.351 lineage has two additional mutations (K417N and E484K) within the RBD region.
source: Both of these mutants carry an N501Y mutation, and the B.1.351 lineage has two additional mutations (K417N and E484K) within the RBD region (Figure 1B,C; Leung et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claim: FDA-authorized mRNA vaccines continued to induce a high level of neutralization against the B.1.1.7 variant.
source: Recent data suggest that the FDA-authorized mRNA vaccines continued to induce a high level of neutralization against the B.1.1.7 variant, but a lower level against B.1.351 variants.
evidence: This claim is based on recent data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: FDA-authorized mRNA vaccines induced a lower level of neutralization against B.1.351 variants.
source: Recent data suggest that the FDA-authorized mRNA vaccines continued to induce a high level of neutralization against the B.1.1.7 variant, but a lower level against B.1.351 variants.
evidence: This claim is based on recent data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Some neutralizing antibodies in phase II/III clinical trials were not able to retain their neutralizing capability against the B.1.351 variant.
source: Several researchers have assessed the neutralization potency of numerous antibodies against the two new variants. Their data suggest that some neutralizing antibodies in phase II/III clinical trials were not able to retain their neutralizing capability against the B.1.351 variant.
evidence: This claim is based on research data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of the RBD–ACE2 complex showed that extensive interactions are formed between RBD and ACE2.
source: The structure of the RBD–ACE2 complex showed that extensive interactions are formed between RBD and ACE2 (Lu et al., 2020; Bauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: ACE2 with a mCherry fused at the C-terminus was located mainly in the cell membrane and endoplasmic reticulum.
source: ACE2 with a mCherry fused at the C-terminus was transfected into HEK293 cells. Confocal microscopic images subsequently showed that ACE2 was located mainly in the cell membrane and endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ACE2–mCherry-positive cells showed co-localization of RBD and ACE2 on the cell surface.
source: ACE2–mCherry-positive cells were stained with AlexaFluor488 labeled-RBD, and the overlay images showed the co-localization of RBD and ACE2 on the cell surface (Figure 1F), validating their interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Kd of RBD from SARS-CoV-2 for ACE2 on the surface of cells is about 50 nM.
source: To measure the binding affinity of RBD from SARS-CoV-2 for ACE2 on the surface of cells, saturation binding was performed using fluorescence flow cytometry by titration of Alexa488-RBD without washing the cells, which yielded a Kd of about 50 nM (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Competition binding assay showed a similar affinity of 50 nM for RBD to ACE2.
source: We also performed a competition-binding assay by titrating unlabeled RBD to compete with 100 nM Alexa488-RBD, which showed a similar affinity of 50 nM (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition binding assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The N501Y mutation from the B.1.1.7 variant showed a fourfold greater affinity than wild-type RBD for the cell surface.
source: The N501Y mutation from the B.1.1.7 variant showed a fourfold greater affinity than wild-type RBD for the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by competition binding assay data.

claim: The N501Y, K417N, E484K triple mutation resulted in an affinity similar to that of the wild type RBD.
source: The mutation resulted in a slightly weaker or similar affinity to cell-surface ACE2, whereas the N501Y, K417N, E484K triple mutation resulted in an affinity similar to that of the wild type RBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by competition binding assay data.

claim: N501Y is the key residue change that increases binding affinity.
source: These results demonstrated that N501Y is the key residue change that increases binding affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding affinity data from competition assays.

claim: RBDN501Y and RBDTriple showed a 10-fold increase in affinity compared to RBD.
source: Compared to RBD, both RBDN501Y and RBDTriple showed a 10-fold increase in affinity, which resulted from a significantly lower off-rate and a slightly higher on-rate (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 10-fold increase in affinity for RBDN501Y and RBDTriple resulted from a significantly lower off-rate and a slightly higher on-rate.
source: Compared to RBD, both RBDN501Y and RBDTriple showed a 10-fold increase in affinity, which resulted from a significantly lower off-rate and a slightly higher on-rate (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR kinetics data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Two other amino acid mutations (K417N and E484K) had less impact on ACE2 binding than N501Y.
source: Two other amino acid mutations (K417N and E484K) had less impact on ACE2 binding, as verified by two single-point mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: N501Y, rather than the other two mutations, is responsible for increasing binding affinity by slowing the rate of dissociation from the ACE2 receptor.
source: This result again emphasized the role of N501Y, rather than the other two mutations, in increasing binding affinity by slowing the rate of dissociation from the ACE2 receptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SPR kinetics data comparing different mutations.

claim: AFM-SMFS is a powerful single-molecule nanotechnology that can be used to manipulate a single molecule or several molecules mechanically.
source: AFM-SMFS is a powerful single-molecule nanotechnology that can be used like optical and magnetic tweezers to manipulate a single molecule or several molecules mechanically (Jobst et al., 2015; Walder et al., 2017; Alonso-Caballero et al., 2021; Löf et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature about AFM-SMFS methodology.

claim: AFM-SMFS has been widely used to study protein mechanics and protein–protein interactions, including the interaction between the spike proteins of viruses and living cells.
source: It has been widely used to study protein mechanics and protein–protein interactions, including the interaction between the spike proteins of viruses and living cells (Kim et al., 2010; Cuellar-Camacho et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Sieben et al., 2012; Alsteens et al., 2017b; Yu et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature about AFM-SMFS applications.

claim: A previous AFM experiment identified the binding events between the wild-type RBD and human ACE2 transfected on A549 cells, obtaining their binding probability and unbinding force/kinetics.
source: A previous AFM experiment identified the binding events between the wild-type RBD and human ACE2 transfected on A549 cells, obtaining their binding probability and unbinding force/kinetics (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: 14% of the events involved a specific interaction between RBDN501Y and ACE2 at a pulling speed of 5 µm/s.
source: For example, 2815 data points on force-extension curves (using a pulling speed of 5 µm/s) have been obtained by probing ACE2-transfected cells with a RBDN501Y-functionalized AFM tip. As indicated by an unbinding force of >20 pN, 14% of the events involved a specific interaction between RBDN501Y and ACE2 (Figure 3D curve 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding probability for RBD with ACE2 was 3.3%.
source: The same experiments and analysis were performed for RBD (3.3%) and RBDTriple (11.2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data.

claim: The binding probability for RBDTriple with ACE2 was 11.2%.
source: The same experiments and analysis were performed for RBD (3.3%) and RBDTriple (11.2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data.

claim: The interaction between RBD and untransfected normal HEK293 cells was 1.7%.
source: The interaction between RBD and untransfected normal HEK293 cells (1.7%) was also measured as a control (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The mean unbinding force for RBD was 49 ± 11 pN (n = 349).
source: The mean unbinding forces for RBD, RBDN501Y, and RBDTriple were 49 ± 11 pN (n = 349), 57 ± 18 pN (n = 394), and 56 ± 12 pN (n = 312), respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mean unbinding force for RBDN501Y was 57 ± 18 pN (n = 394).
source: The mean unbinding forces for RBD, RBDN501Y, and RBDTriple were 49 ± 11 pN (n = 349), 57 ± 18 pN (n = 394), and 56 ± 12 pN (n = 312), respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mean unbinding force for RBDTriple was 56 ± 12 pN (n = 312).
source: The mean unbinding forces for RBD, RBDN501Y, and RBDTriple were 49 ± 11 pN (n = 349), 57 ± 18 pN (n = 394), and 56 ± 12 pN (n = 312), respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both RBD mutants showed a higher binding probability and unbinding force than the wild type.
source: Both RBD mutants showed a higher binding probability and unbinding force than the wild type, while the properties of the two variants are similar to each other (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: The properties of the two variants (RBDN501Y and RBDTriple) are similar to each other.
source: Both RBD mutants showed a higher binding probability and unbinding force than the wild type, while the properties of the two variants are similar to each other (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: RBDK417N showed an unbinding force of 40 ± 11 pN (n = 894).
source: Finally, we also performed AFM measurements on RBDK417N (40 ± 11 pN, n = 894) and RBDE484K (41 ± 11 pN, n = 606) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: RBDE484K showed an unbinding force of 41 ± 11 pN (n = 606).
source: Finally, we also performed AFM measurements on RBDK417N (40 ± 11 pN, n = 894) and RBDE484K (41 ± 11 pN, n = 606) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: RBDK417N and RBDE484K showed weaker unbinding forces than wild type RBD.
source: These mutant RBDs showed weaker unbinding forces than wild type RBD, in agreement with previous ensemble measurements and verifying our single-molecule results.
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS experimental data and is consistent with other measurements.

claim: According to the Bell–Evans model, the force that is externally applied by AFM lowers the unbinding activation energy.
source: According to the Bell–Evans model, the force that is externally applied by AFM lowers the unbinding activation energy (Merkel et al., 1999; Yu et al., 2017; Zheng and Li, 2011; Garcia-Manyes and Beedle, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature about the Bell-Evans model.

claim: The binding strength of the ligand–receptor bond is proportional to the logarithm of the loading rate.
source: Thus, the binding strength of the ligand–receptor bond (i.e. interaction) is proportional to the logarithm of the loading rate, which describes the effect of the force applied on the bond over time.
evidence: This is a principle of the Bell-Evans model.

claim: The koff of RBDN501Y is 0.030 ± 0.017 s−1.
source: Similarly, the koff of the two RBD mutants are close to each other (0.030 ± 0.017 s−1 and 0.035 ± 0.024  s−1) but slower than that of the wild-type RBD (0.075 ± 0.048  s−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS data fitted to the Bell-Evans model.

claim: The koff of RBDTriple is 0.035 ± 0.024 s−1.
source: Similarly, the koff of the two RBD mutants are close to each other (0.030 ± 0.017 s−1 and 0.035 ± 0.024  s−1) but slower than that of the wild-type RBD (0.075 ± 0.048  s−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS data fitted to the Bell-Evans model.

claim: The koff of wild-type RBD is 0.075 ± 0.048 s−1.
source: Similarly, the koff of the two RBD mutants are close to each other (0.030 ± 0.017 s−1 and 0.035 ± 0.024  s−1) but slower than that of the wild-type RBD (0.075 ± 0.048  s−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS data fitted to the Bell-Evans model.

claim: The koff of the two RBD mutants are slower than that of the wild-type RBD.
source: Similarly, the koff of the two RBD mutants are close to each other (0.030 ± 0.017 s−1 and 0.035 ± 0.024  s−1) but slower than that of the wild-type RBD (0.075 ± 0.048  s−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM-SMFS data fitted to the Bell-Evans model.

claim: In the wild-type RBD–ACE2 interaction, T500 forms two hydrogen bonds with Y41 and D355 from ACE2.
source: In the wild-type RBD–ACE2 interaction, T500 forms two hydrogen bonds with Y41 and D355 from ACE2; K417 from RBD forms a salt bridge with D30 from ACE2; and N487 forms one hydrogen bond with Y83 (Figure 4A, snapshot 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: K417 from RBD forms a salt bridge with D30 from ACE2.
source: In the wild-type RBD–ACE2 interaction, T500 forms two hydrogen bonds with Y41 and D355 from ACE2; K417 from RBD forms a salt bridge with D30 from ACE2; and N487 forms one hydrogen bond with Y83 (Figure 4A, snapshot 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: N487 forms one hydrogen bond with Y83.
source: In the wild-type RBD–ACE2 interaction, T500 forms two hydrogen bonds with Y41 and D355 from ACE2; K417 from RBD forms a salt bridge with D30 from ACE2; and N487 forms one hydrogen bond with Y83 (Figure 4A, snapshot 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rupture force for the wild-type RBD-ACE2 complex was simulated as 427 ± 58 pN (n = 20).
source: This force was defined as the rupture or disassociation force for the complex and was simulated as 427 ± 58 pN (n = 20, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the RBDN501Y–ACE2 complex, Y501 forms an additional π-π interaction with Y41 and an additional π-cation interaction with K353.
source: In the RBDN501Y–ACE2 complex, Y501 forms an additional π-π interaction with Y41 and an additional π-cation interaction with K353 (Figure 4B, snapshot 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: An elevated unbinding force of 499 ± 67 pN (n = 20) was obtained for the complex between RBDN501Y and ACE2 compared to that for the complex between wild-type RBD and ACE2 (p=8.29 e–4).
source: An elevated unbinding force of 499 ± 67 pN (n = 20) was obtained for the complex between RBDN501Y and ACE2 compared to that for the complex between wild-type RBD and ACE2 (p=8.29 e–4, Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RBDTriple might have a stronger contact than wild-type RBD with ACE2.
source: Similarly, SMD simulations revealed that RBDTriple might also have a stronger contact than wild-type RBD with ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference based on SMD simulation results.

claim: The unbinding force for RBDTriple was 521 ± 65 pN (p=2.33 e–5).
source: The unbinding force was 521 ± 65 pN (p=2.33 e–5, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For the wild-type RBD–ACE2 complex, the distances between residue N501 and residues Y41 and K353 increased significantly at a shorter extension along the pulling pathway at the distance of 2.2 ± 0.7 nm (n = 20).
source: For the wild-type RBD–ACE2 complex, the distances between residue N501 and residues Y41 (Figure 4D) and K353 (Figure 4E) increased significantly at a shorter extension along the pulling pathway (purple line) at the distance of 2.2 ± 0.7 nm (n = 20), indicating no interaction between these residues in the RBD–ACE2 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: For RBDN501Y, the distances showed a smaller increase at an extension of 2.9 ± 0.8 nm (p=5.38 e–3, n = 20).
source: For the two variants (Figure 4D,E), the distances showed a smaller increase at an extension of 2.9 ± 0.8 nm (p=5.38 e–3, orange line, n = 20) and 3.3 ± 0.8 nm (p=6.39 e–5, green line, n = 20), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: For RBDTriple, the distances showed a smaller increase at an extension of 3.3 ± 0.8 nm (p=6.39 e–5, n = 20).
source: For the two variants (Figure 4D,E), the distances showed a smaller increase at an extension of 2.9 ± 0.8 nm (p=5.38 e–3, orange line, n = 20) and 3.3 ± 0.8 nm (p=6.39 e–5, green line, n = 20), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by SMD simulation data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: SMD simulations demonstrate that the RBDN501Y–ACE2 and RBDTriple–ACE2 complexes have a higher unbinding force than wild-type RBD–ACE2 complexes.
